Reference: Loumeau (2024)

Model Setting

The paper asks whether New Towns, planned large urban sub-centres, are a good way to accommodate rising urbanisation. Since 1900, 785 metropolitan areas have developed New Towns, with an average target population of 264,436 residents. Their rationale is the co-location hypothesis: decentralising jobs and housing into sub-centres improves the spatial match between residence and workplace and shortens commutes. Reduced-form studies cannot separate this pure urban-structure effect from other equilibrium responses, in particular from induced population growth. The paper builds a quantitative spatial general equilibrium model in the spirit of Ahlfeldt, Redding, Sturm and Wolf (2015), designed for large-scale urban master plans. A master plan has three components: location-specific availability of residential and commercial land, investments in the metropolitan transport network, and a head tax that finances both. Heterogeneous workers choose a residence-workplace pair, firms of different sectors compete for commercial floor space, and, as in Heblich, Redding and Sturm (2020), the metropolitan area is an open city embedded in a national economy, so that its population responds to welfare inside the area relative to a reservation utility outside.

The application is the five New Towns of the Paris metropolitan area (Cergy-Pontoise, Evry, Marne-la-Vallee, Melun-Senart and St-Quentin-en-Yvelines, 70 municipalities in total), built from 1969 under the 1965 master plan and connected to the historical centre by the rapid suburban rail network (RER lines A to D). The government secured 44,862 hectares of building land, of which 24,086 hectares were bought at an average of 13.04 francs per square metre, and 184,238 housing units were built in the New Towns between 1969 and 1990. The calibrated model compares the observed plan with three alternative plans that distribute the same total amount of new land differently. By 2015, relative to a plan that scales up the 1968 land distribution, New Towns raise metropolitan population by 18.46 percent (868,628 residents), raise metropolitan GDP by 11.4 percent (3.27 billion euros) and lower average commuting time by 6.9 percent (0.86 minutes). Because the population effect dominates, total commuting time rises by 10.29 percent. The 2015 census counts slightly more than 800,000 residents in the New Towns, fewer than the induced population, so the New Towns “generated” their own occupants and did not accommodate pre-existing urban growth, a land-use counterpart of the fundamental law of highway congestion. Without the accompanying transport investments the New Town plan is dominated by the scaled-up plan. A difference-in-differences analysis of 314 New Towns opened worldwide between 1992 and 2012 gives a GDP effect of about 10.5 percent, close to the structural estimate for Paris.

Environment and Urban Master Plan

The metropolitan area consists of locations i∈{1,…,I}i\in\{1,\dots,I\}i∈{1,…,I}. Time ttt is discrete and each period is self-contained. Workers are heterogeneous, with types θ∈Θ\theta\in\Thetaθ∈Θ. The national economy has an exogenous mass of workers HMtH_{\mathbb{M}t}HMt​, of which the endogenous mass HNtH_{\mathbb{N}t}HNt​ lives in the metropolitan area; there is no commuting across its border. An urban master plan MMM specifies the residential land LRitML^M_{Rit}LRitM​ available in location iii and the commercial land LCjtML^M_{Cjt}LCjtM​ available in location jjj, both weakly increasing over time, so that in each period the planner only decides where to place the newly available land. The plan superscript is dropped below. The plan is financed by a head tax ϕ\phiϕ on all workers, which is non-distorting given the equilibrium population.

The transport network has two layers. An exogenous road network connects every municipality to its neighbours. In addition the planner builds fast segments (suburban rapid railways) that connect each New Town to the core. The route of each segment is the path (i1,i2,…,in)(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n)(i1​,i2​,…,in​) from iii to i′i'i′ on an undirected graph, with Euclidean edge lengths eii′=∣∣ii′∣∣e_{ii'}=||ii'||eii′​=∣∣ii′∣∣, that solves the shortest path problem:

min⁡i1,i2,…,in∑i=1n−1f(ei,i+1)(6.5.2.1)\min_{i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n}\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}f\left(e_{i,i+1}\right) \tag{6.5.2.1}i1​,i2​,…,in​min​i=1∑n−1​f(ei,i+1​)(6.5.2.1)

which is solved with the algorithm of Dijkstra (1959). Locations between a New Town and the centre benefit incidentally from these segments, a feature used later for identification. Commuters take the faster of the route on the local network and the route that uses the fast segments. Developers use all the land that the plan makes available, at land cost rRitr_{Rit}rRit​, and turn it into floor space:

lRit=LRitγ(6.5.2.2)l_{Rit}=L^{\gamma}_{Rit} \tag{6.5.2.2}lRit​=LRitγ​(6.5.2.2)

with the same technology for commercial floor space. Floor space is rented to residents and firms at market prices.

This is the channel through which New Towns induce urbanisation.

Floor Space Markets and Equilibrium

Developers own the floor space and rent it out. Residential floor space supplied to type θ\thetaθ in location iii is the share ΩRitθ\Omega^{\theta}_{Rit}ΩRitθ​ of the local stock, and it equals the Cobb-Douglas demand of the residents of that type:

lRitθ=ΩRitθlRit=(1−β)E[wjtθ∣i]hitθQ~it(6.5.2.15)l^{\theta}_{Rit}=\Omega^{\theta}_{Rit}l_{Rit}=\left(1-\beta\right)\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[w^{\theta}_{jt}|i\right]h^{\theta}_{it}}{\tilde{Q}_{it}} \tag{6.5.2.15}lRitθ​=ΩRitθ​lRit​=(1−β)Q~​it​E[wjtθ​∣i]hitθ​​(6.5.2.15)

where hitθh^{\theta}_{it}hitθ​ is the number of residents of type θ\thetaθ in iii and the expectation is the average wage of these residents over their workplaces. The shares ΩRitθ\Omega^{\theta}_{Rit}ΩRitθ​ sum to one across types in every location. Firms of different types likewise compete for commercial floor space, with shares ΩCjtθ\Omega^{\theta}_{Cjt}ΩCjtθ​ that sum to one. Both markets clear when all types face the same price in a location:

Qit=Qitθ,qjt=qjtθ,∀θ∈Θ, ∀i,j∈I(6.5.2.16)Q_{it}=Q^{\theta}_{it},\qquad q_{jt}=q^{\theta}_{jt},\qquad\forall\theta\in\Theta,\ \forall i,j\in I \tag{6.5.2.16}Qit​=Qitθ​,qjt​=qjtθ​,∀θ∈Θ, ∀i,j∈I(6.5.2.16)

Since the zero-profit floor price depends on wjtθw^{\theta}_{jt}wjtθ​ and TjθT^{\theta}_jTjθ​, equality of commercial prices across types ties each type's wage in jjj to its own productivity there.

Proposition 1. With strictly positive, finite and exogenous location characteristics, for each period there exist unique general equilibrium vectors of residence and workplace probabilities, residential and commercial floor space used by each type, floor prices QQQ and qqq, wages wθw^{\theta}wθ, floor space shares ΩRθ\Omega^{\theta}_RΩRθ​ and ΩCθ\Omega^{\theta}_CΩCθ​, and subsidy terms sθs^{\theta}sθ, together with unique scalars HNθH^{\theta}_{\mathbb{N}}HNθ​ for each type and ϕ\phiϕ. The proof is in the online appendix. Uniqueness rests on the absence of contemporaneous spillovers: biθb^{\theta}_ibiθ​ and TjθT^{\theta}_jTjθ​ are exogenous in the baseline, so the only forces are dispersion forces (inelastic floor space and commuting costs) and the idiosyncratic shocks. Because each period is self-contained, a counterfactual is a sequence of static equilibria that differ in land availability, transport network and head tax.

Calibration

Geography and types. The metropolitan area is delineated with the City Clustering Algorithm of Rozenfeld et al. (2011) on 2015 municipal population: starting from Paris, the cluster grows by adding all municipalities within 10 km whose density exceeds 5 inhabitants per square kilometre, the average density 100 km from the centre. Census population and employment are observed in 1968, 1990 and 2015 and are paired with housing stocks of 1971, 1990 and 2013. There are six types, the product of three demographic groups (juniors aged 20 to 30; families, that is, workers aged 15 to 20 and 30 to 50; seniors above 50) and two sectors (manufacturing and services), ordered from juniors in manufacturing (θ=1\theta=1θ=1) to seniors in services (θ=6\theta=6θ=6).

Parameters from the literature. The Frechet shape parameter is ϵ=6.83\epsilon=6.83ϵ=6.83 from Ahlfeldt, Redding, Sturm and Wolf (2015). The expenditure share of the final good is β=0.78\beta=0.78β=0.78, consistent with Davis and Ortalo-Magne (2011). The labour share is αθ=0.75\alpha_{\theta}=0.75αθ​=0.75 for the manufacturing types (θ<4\theta<4θ<4) and αθ=0.8\alpha_{\theta}=0.8αθ​=0.8 for the service types (θ≥4\theta\geq4θ≥4), from the French statistical office. The exponent that turns land into floor space is γ=0.9\gamma=0.9γ=0.9. Housing units are converted into floor space at the regional average of 57 square metres per unit. The 1969 land price per square metre is a quadratic function of distance to the Hotel de Ville with intercept 24.928, linear coefficient −1.63-1.63−1.63 and quadratic coefficient 0.019; francs are converted at 0.15 euro with 2.5 percent inflation. Public infrastructure adds 30 percent to land purchase costs, and the head tax is annualised over 50 years.

Commuting costs. The travel time τij\tau_{ij}τij​ is the shortest time in minutes on the network, which combines 35,735 road segments as of 2015 (effective speed 30 km/h, with a congestion rate of 39 percent) and the RER (49.6 km/h), including access to the nearest station. Commuting costs are exponential in travel time:

dijθ=exp⁡(ξθτij)(6.5.2.17)d^{\theta}_{ij}=\exp\left(\xi^{\theta}\tau_{ij}\right) \tag{6.5.2.17}dijθ​=exp(ξθτij​)(6.5.2.17)

with τii=1\tau_{ii}=1τii​=1. The commuting probabilities then give a semi-log gravity equation:

ln⁡πijθ=κθτij+ωiθ+ζjθ+εijθ(6.5.2.18)\ln\pi^{\theta}_{ij}=\kappa^{\theta}\tau_{ij}+\omega^{\theta}_i+\zeta^{\theta}_j+\varepsilon^{\theta}_{ij} \tag{6.5.2.18}lnπijθ​=κθτij​+ωiθ​+ζjθ​+εijθ​(6.5.2.18)

where ωiθ\omega^{\theta}_iωiθ​ and ζjθ\zeta^{\theta}_jζjθ​ are residence and workplace fixed effects and πijθ\pi^{\theta}_{ij}πijθ​ is observed in 2010 from individual commuting data aggregated to municipality pairs by type. The paper writes the travel-cost parameter as κθ=ξθ×ϵ\kappa^{\theta}=\xi^{\theta}\times\epsilonκθ=ξθ×ϵ; since vijtθv^{\theta}_{ijt}vijtθ​ is proportional to dijθd^{\theta}_{ij}dijθ​ to the power −ϵ-\epsilon−ϵ, the coefficient in the gravity equation as written equals −ξθϵ-\xi^{\theta}\epsilon−ξθϵ, so the relation holds in absolute value. The identification problem is that transport links are placed to connect non-random places. The paper uses an incidental treatment design: the set OOO of municipalities that lie along the RER between the historical centre and a New Town were connected but were not the target of the investment. Estimating the gravity equation on commutes between municipalities in OOO, by Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood and by negative binomial regression, gives semi-elasticities that are larger in magnitude than in the full sample, which is read as evidence of strategic placement. Manufacturing workers are less sensitive to commuting time than service workers, and juniors are less sensitive than families and seniors within each sector. The estimates themselves are reported only in the online appendix.

Model inversion. Given ϵ\epsilonϵ, the κθ\kappa^{\theta}κθ, travel times and observed employment by workplace hCθh^{\theta}_ChCθ​ and by residence hRθh^{\theta}_RhRθ​, the commuting market clearing condition (workplace employment of a type equals the sum over residences of residents times their conditional probability of commuting to that workplace) is solved for the wage vectors wθw^{\theta}wθ, up to scale. Given wages and the observed commercial price qqq, the first-order and zero-profit conditions give productivities TθT^{\theta}Tθ and commercial floor space lCθl^{\theta}_ClCθ​ uniquely. Given wages, observed residents, subsidies and housing prices QQQ, the residential choice probabilities give amenities bθb^{\theta}bθ, unique up to a normalisation. The last two steps are independent of each other. Finally the open-city condition is solved for Uˉtθ\bar{U}^{\theta}_tUˉtθ​ using national and metropolitan population by type in each period. As a test on an untargeted moment, predicted municipal GDP in 2015 lines up with observed GDP close to the 45-degree line.

Alternative Master Plans

All plans release the same total amount of new residential and commercial land in each period; a tilde denotes the increment of a period. Under the scaled-up plan (su), the status quo benchmark, new land follows the 1968 distribution:

Let sts_tst​ denote the part of new land that the observed plan places in New Towns. Under the hyper-concentration plan (hc) this part is allocated in inverse proportion to the great-circle distance di,Parisd_{i,Paris}di,Paris​ to the Hotel de Ville:

and under the urban sprawl plan (us) it is allocated in proportion to the area aia_iai​ of each municipality:

L~itR,us=stai∑iai∑iL~itR,us+(1−st)L~itR,su(6.5.2.21)\tilde{L}^{R,us}_{it}=s_t\frac{a_i}{\sum_ia_i}\sum_i\tilde{L}^{R,us}_{it}+\left(1-s_t\right)\tilde{L}^{R,su}_{it} \tag{6.5.2.21}L~itR,us​=st​∑i​ai​ai​​i∑​L~itR,us​+(1−st​)L~itR,su​(6.5.2.21)

In the paper the last term of both formulas is printed as (1−st)∑iL~itR,su(1-s_t)\sum_i\tilde{L}^{R,su}_{it}(1−st​)∑i​L~itR,su​, a metropolitan total, which cannot be right for a location-specific allocation: summing over iii would violate the equal-total requirement. The version above, with sts_tst​ read as a share, adds up. The same rules apply to commercial land. Outcomes are compared in the long run (2015): population, GDP (the sum of wages across workers), average and total commuting time, the average rateable value of residential and commercial floor space, and residential mixity. Mixity of location iii is the entropy index:

ei=−∑θ=1Θπiθlog⁡πiθ(6.5.2.22)e_i=-\sum_{\theta=1}^{\Theta}\pi^{\theta}_i\log\pi^{\theta}_i \tag{6.5.2.22}ei​=−θ=1∑Θ​πiθ​logπiθ​(6.5.2.22)

where πiθ\pi^{\theta}_iπiθ​ is the share of type θ\thetaθ among residents of iii; the metropolitan measure is the population-weighted average.

Counterfactual Results

All numbers are the effect of the observed New Town plan relative to the stated alternative, by 2015.

  • Relative to the scaled-up plan: population +18.46+18.46+18.46 percent (868,628 residents), GDP +11.4+11.4+11.4 percent (3.27 billion euros), average commuting time −6.9-6.9−6.9 percent (−0.86-0.86−0.86 minutes), total commuting time +10.29+10.29+10.29 percent, average rateable value +2.89+2.89+2.89 percent (0.59 euros per square metre), mixity −0.67-0.67−0.67 percent. Higher rents and more segregation are the unintended consequences of denser and more homogeneous neighbourhoods.

  • Relative to hyper-concentration: population +22.05+22.05+22.05 percent (1,037,579), GDP +14.21+14.21+14.21 percent (4.08 billion euros), average commuting −6.15-6.15−6.15 percent (−0.76-0.76−0.76 minutes), total commuting +14.55+14.55+14.55 percent, rateable value +2.72+2.72+2.72 percent, mixity −0.78-0.78−0.78 percent.

  • Relative to urban sprawl: population +71.81+71.81+71.81 percent (3,378,259), GDP +63.87+63.87+63.87 percent (18.33 billion euros), average commuting −8.28-8.28−8.28 percent (−1.05-1.05−1.05 minutes), total commuting +57.59+57.59+57.59 percent, rateable value −4.06-4.06−4.06 percent, mixity −0.43-0.43−0.43 percent. Sprawl is the worst plan for population.

  • New Towns without the transport investments (relative to scaled-up): population −11.84-11.84−11.84 percent (−556,901-556,901−556,901), GDP −16.19-16.19−16.19 percent (−4.65-4.65−4.65 billion euros), average commuting +3.06+3.06+3.06 percent (+0.38+0.38+0.38 minutes), total commuting −9.14-9.14−9.14 percent. Without an efficient network, New Towns harm the metropolitan area.

  • Road congestion halved (from 39 to 19.5 percent): the advantage of New Towns over the scaled-up plan remains, with population +11.97+11.97+11.97 percent (563,365), GDP +5.36+5.36+5.36 percent (1.54 billion euros), average commuting −5.22-5.22−5.22 percent and total commuting +6.13+6.13+6.13 percent.

  • Composition: relative to the scaled-up plan, families grow by 21.56 percent, juniors by 18.48 percent and seniors by 16.65 percent; manufacturing workers grow by 25.7 percent and service workers by 16.62 percent, in line with the sorting of families and manufacturing workers into New Towns seen in the raw data.

Agglomeration, Closed City and Robustness

The baseline has no spillovers. An extension replaces the fundamentals by density-dependent terms as in Ahlfeldt, Redding, Sturm and Wolf (2015). Writing kkk for the index of summation (the paper reuses the index of the location itself, which is a misprint):

Tjtθ=Tjθ[∑k=1Ie−δτjk(hCktθlCktθ)]λ,bitθ=biθ[∑k=1Ie−ρτik(hRktθlRktθ)]η(6.5.2.23)T^{\theta}_{jt}=T^{\theta}_j\left[\sum_{k=1}^{I}e^{-\delta\tau_{jk}}\left(\frac{h^{\theta}_{Ckt}}{l^{\theta}_{Ckt}}\right)\right]^{\lambda},\qquad b^{\theta}_{it}=b^{\theta}_i\left[\sum_{k=1}^{I}e^{-\rho\tau_{ik}}\left(\frac{h^{\theta}_{Rkt}}{l^{\theta}_{Rkt}}\right)\right]^{\eta} \tag{6.5.2.23}Tjtθ​=Tjθ​[k=1∑I​e−δτjk​(lCktθ​hCktθ​​)]λ,bitθ​=biθ​[k=1∑I​e−ρτik​(lRktθ​hRktθ​​)]η(6.5.2.23)

with decay parameters δ=0.98\delta=0.98δ=0.98 and ρ=0.55\rho=0.55ρ=0.55. The model, including the reservation utilities, is recalibrated for each pair of spillover elasticities λ\lambdaλ and η\etaη, which are raised symmetrically. The gains from New Towns in population, GDP and average commuting time grow with the strength of spillovers, though multiple equilibria then become possible. Because the provision of schools and hospitals is almost linear in the residential externality term, this exercise also stands in for endogenous local public services. In a closed city with exogenous population, the gains in GDP and average commuting time disappear, with or without agglomeration economies. The benefits of New Towns therefore operate through induced urbanisation, and would be small in countries where little potential for further urban growth remains. The direction of all results is stable for ϵ\epsilonϵ between 1 and 8 and for alternative density thresholds of the clustering algorithm.

Reduced-Form Evidence

Two reduced-form exercises frame the model. For Paris, municipalities in the five New Towns are compared with those in the planned but discarded New Towns:

yit=∑t=t‾tˉβtDit+μi+ηt+uit(6.5.2.24)y_{it}=\sum_{t=\underline{t}}^{\bar{t}}\beta_tD_{it}+\mu_i+\eta_t+u_{it} \tag{6.5.2.24}yit​=t=t​∑tˉ​βt​Dit​+μi​+ηt​+uit​(6.5.2.24)

where yity_{it}yit​ is an outcome of municipality iii in census year ttt, DitD_{it}Dit​ interacts year indicators with treatment, and μi\mu_iμi​ and ηt\eta_tηt​ are fixed effects, with 1962 as the reference year. By 2015 the average New Town municipality had grown almost 15 times more than the control municipalities, and the shares of families and of manufacturing workers rose. Metropolitan commuting times grew more slowly after the New Towns opened while population growth was stable and job concentration fell.

For external validity, cells of about one square kilometre in urban areas that received a New Town between 1992 and 2012 are compared with cells in other urban areas (3,598 urban areas, 281,280 cells, 3,094,080 cell-year observations):

log⁡yitp=∑p=p‾pˉβpDip+μi+ηt+uitp(6.5.2.25)\log y_{itp}=\sum_{p=\underline{p}}^{\bar{p}}\beta_pD_{ip}+\mu_i+\eta_t+u_{itp} \tag{6.5.2.25}logyitp​=p=p​∑pˉ​​βp​Dip​+μi​+ηt​+uitp​(6.5.2.25)

where yitpy_{itp}yitp​ is night-time luminosity and DipD_{ip}Dip​ interacts treatment with pooled event-time indicators ppp around the opening of the New Town. Observed luminosity litl_{it}lit​ is a doubly censored version of a latent normal variable lit∗l^*_{it}lit∗​, which motivates a Tobit specification:

lit={0if lit∗≤0lit∗if 0<lit∗≤6363if lit∗>63(6.5.2.26)l_{it}=\begin{cases}0&\text{if }l^*_{it}\leq0\\l^*_{it}&\text{if }0<l^*_{it}\leq63\\63&\text{if }l^*_{it}>63\end{cases} \tag{6.5.2.26}lit​=⎩⎨⎧​0lit∗​63​if lit∗​≤0if 0<lit∗​≤63if lit∗​>63​(6.5.2.26)

Treated and control areas evolve in parallel until about four years before the opening. Ten years after it, luminosity is about 35 percent higher (a coefficient of 0.3). With an elasticity of GDP to night lights of 0.3 from Henderson, Storeygard and Weil (2012), this is GDP growth of about 10.5 percent, close to the 11.4 percent of the structural model. Estimators that ignore the censoring give smaller effects.

This is the planner's routing problem for one fast transport segment (a rapid suburban railway line). The objects are vertices of an undirected graph of locations. A candidate route is an ordered list of vertices (i1,i2,…,in)(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n)(i1​,i2​,…,in​) whose first element is the origin (the core urban centre) and whose last element is the destination (a New Town). The number of vertices nnn is itself chosen, since a route may pass through few or many intermediate locations. Each edge has a length eii′=∣∣ii′∣∣e_{ii'}=||ii'||eii′​=∣∣ii′∣∣, the Euclidean distance between its two end points, and f(⋅)f(\cdot)f(⋅) turns a length into a cost. The objective adds the cost of the n−1n-1n−1 consecutive edges of the route.

The notation is compressed: the summation index iii counts positions along the route, so ei,i+1e_{i,i+1}ei,i+1​ stands for the edge between the vertex in position iii and the vertex in position i+1i+1i+1. Written out with a position index mmm (not in the note), the objective is

∑m=1n−1f(eim,im+1)\sum_{m=1}^{n-1}f\left(e_{i_m,i_{m+1}}\right)m=1∑n−1​f(eim​,im+1​​)

The paper does not specify fff. If fff is the identity, the solution is the route of smallest total Euclidean length, which is what the paper calls a Euclidean single-pair shortest path. Because f≥0f\geq0f≥0, the problem is solved exactly by the algorithm of Dijkstra (1959), which expands outward from the origin and fixes the cheapest cost to one more vertex at each step.

The economic role of this equation is twofold. First, it makes the transport part of a master plan a mechanical function of where the New Towns are placed, so that the counterfactual plans do not require a separate choice of rail routes. Second, the locations that happen to lie on the cheapest route between the centre and a New Town receive a station although they were not the target. This set of incidentally treated municipalities, called OOO in the note, is the source of identification for the gravity equation (18). The resulting network enters the model only through the travel times τij\tau_{ij}τij​ in equation (17).

This is the technology of floor space developers. LRitL_{Rit}LRit​ is the residential land that the master plan makes available in location iii in period ttt (a policy variable, in units of land area), and lRitl_{Rit}lRit​ is the resulting stock of residential floor space. The same function, with CCC in place of RRR, gives commercial floor space lCjtl_{Cjt}lCjt​ from commercial land LCjtL_{Cjt}LCjt​. Developers are assumed to use all the land that is released, so floor space supply in each location is fixed by the plan and does not respond to floor prices within a period.

The parameter γ\gammaγ is the elasticity of floor space with respect to land:

∂ln⁡lRit∂ln⁡LRit=γ,∂lRit∂LRit=γLRitγ−1\frac{\partial\ln l_{Rit}}{\partial\ln L_{Rit}}=\gamma,\qquad\frac{\partial l_{Rit}}{\partial L_{Rit}}=\gamma L^{\gamma-1}_{Rit}∂lnLRit​∂lnlRit​​=γ,∂LRit​∂lRit​​=γLRitγ−1​

With the calibrated value γ=0.9\gamma=0.9γ=0.9 the technology is concave: doubling the land of a location raises its floor space by the factor 20.9≈1.872^{0.9}\approx1.8720.9≈1.87, and the marginal hectare yields less floor space where much land is already in use. Relative to Ahlfeldt, Redding, Sturm and Wolf (2015), where floor space is produced from land and capital, the capital input is suppressed and land is the only input.

This functional form buys two things. It maps each counterfactual land allocation in equations (19) to (21) directly into a vector of floor space supplies, and its concavity means that the spatial distribution of a fixed total of land matters for the total amount of floor space: for a given total, spreading land evenly produces more floor space than concentrating it. The fixed supply lRitl_{Rit}lRit​ then enters the residential market clearing condition (15), where the price QitQ_{it}Qit​ adjusts, and it is one of the dispersion forces behind the uniqueness result of Proposition 1. The land cost rRitr_{Rit}rRit​ does not affect the quantity; it only enters the cost of the plan that the head tax ϕ\phiϕ in equation (5) must cover.

This is the direct utility of worker ω\omegaω of type θ\thetaθ who lives in iii and works in jjj. Utility is linear in the index CijtωθC^{\theta}_{ijt\omega}Cijtωθ​, so the index is the utility level. It has four parts. The Cobb-Douglas aggregate combines the final good cijtωθc^{\theta}_{ijt\omega}cijtωθ​ (the numeraire) and residential floor space lRijtωθl^{\theta}_{Rijt\omega}lRijtωθ​ with expenditure shares β\betaβ and 1−β1-\beta1−β; the calibration uses β=0.78\beta=0.78β=0.78, so 22 percent of income is spent on housing. The amenity biθ>0b^{\theta}_i>0biθ​>0 scales utility up and depends on the residence and on the type, so a junior and a family can value the same municipality differently. The commuting cost dijθ≥1d^{\theta}_{ij}\geq1dijθ​≥1 scales utility down and depends on the pair and on the type; it is an iceberg cost in utility, not a money or time cost in the budget. The shock zijtωθz^{\theta}_{ijt\omega}zijtωθ​ is the worker's idiosyncratic taste for the pair, with the distribution in equation (4).

The constants β−β\beta^{-\beta}β−β and (1−β)−(1−β)(1-\beta)^{-(1-\beta)}(1−β)−(1−β) are a normalisation. They are chosen so that the indirect utility has no constant in front, since at the optimum of the Cobb-Douglas problem with income mmm and housing price QQQ

(βmβ)β((1−β)m/Q1−β)1−β=mQβ−1\left(\frac{\beta m}{\beta}\right)^{\beta}\left(\frac{(1-\beta)m/Q}{1-\beta}\right)^{1-\beta}=mQ^{\beta-1}(ββm​)β(1−β(1−β)m/Q​)1−β=mQβ−1

This is the step that leads to equation (6). The paper uses the same kind of normalisation in the production function (11), but there it does not carry it through to the first-order conditions, as discussed under equations (12) to (14).

The multiplicative structure is what makes the model tractable: amenity, commuting cost, income and housing price enter as a product, so that with a Frechet shock the choice probabilities in equation (8) have a closed form. It rules out income effects in the housing share (homothetic preferences) and any direct interaction between commuting and consumption.

This is the cumulative distribution function of the idiosyncratic shock: the probability that the taste draw of worker ω\omegaω for the residence-workplace pair (i,j)(i,j)(i,j) is at most a given value. It is a Frechet (type II extreme value) distribution with shape parameter ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0 and scale normalised to one, following Eaton and Kortum (2002). Draws are independent across workers and across pairs, and the same ϵ\epsilonϵ applies to all types θ\thetaθ. The support is the positive real line.

The shape parameter governs dispersion. A larger ϵ\epsilonϵ means that draws are more concentrated, workers are more alike, and choices respond more strongly to differences in the systematic part of utility. The density and the mean (which exists only for ϵ>1\epsilon>1ϵ>1) are

F′(z)=ϵz−ϵ−1e−z−ϵ,E[z]=Γ(ϵ−1ϵ)F'(z)=\epsilon z^{-\epsilon-1}e^{-z^{-\epsilon}},\qquad\mathbb{E}[z]=\Gamma\left(\frac{\epsilon-1}{\epsilon}\right)F′(z)=ϵz−ϵ−1e−z−ϵ,E[z]=Γ(ϵϵ−1​)

which is where the Gamma function in equation (10) comes from. With the calibrated value ϵ=6.83\epsilon=6.83ϵ=6.83 the mean is about 1.121.121.12.

Two properties are used later. First, a Frechet variable multiplied by a positive constant is again Frechet with the same shape, so the indirect utility (6) is Frechet with a scale that equals the attractiveness vijtθv^{\theta}_{ijt}vijtθ​ of equation (7). Second, the maximum of independent Frechet variables with a common shape is Frechet with scale equal to the sum of the scales. Together they give the choice probabilities (8) and (9), with ϵ\epsilonϵ as the elasticity of the odds of choosing a pair with respect to its systematic utility, and the expected utility on the right-hand side of the open-city condition (10), where ϵ\epsilonϵ becomes the elasticity of metropolitan population with respect to expected utility. In the gravity equation (18) ϵ\epsilonϵ multiplies the commuting parameter ξθ\xi^{\theta}ξθ, which is why only the product is identified from commuting flows and ϵ\epsilonϵ is taken from the literature.

These two definitions describe how the master plan and housing policy enter the budget of a worker of type θ\thetaθ.

The first is the after-tax wage. wjtθw^{\theta}_{jt}wjtθ​ is the wage paid to type θ\thetaθ at workplace jjj and ϕ\phiϕ is the head tax that finances the land purchases and infrastructure of the plan. The tax is the same amount for every worker, whatever the type, residence or workplace. It is called non-distorting because, for a given metropolitan population, it is a lump sum. It is still not neutral for location choices in this model: utility is proportional to w~jtθ\tilde{w}^{\theta}_{jt}w~jtθ​, so subtracting a constant lowers the after-tax wage proportionally more at low-wage workplaces, and it lowers the expected utility of living in the metropolitan area in equation (10), which reduces the population. The definition requires wjtθ>ϕw^{\theta}_{jt}>\phiwjtθ​>ϕ.

The second is the effective housing price. QiQ_iQi​ is the market price of residential floor space and siθs^{\theta}_isiθ​ is a type- and location-specific subsidy term that multiplies it. The paper writes this definition without the time subscript; elsewhere the same objects appear as QitQ_{it}Qit​, sitθs^{\theta}_{it}sitθ​ and Q~it\tilde{Q}_{it}Q~​it​. The sign convention is the reverse of the usual one: a higher sitθs^{\theta}_{it}sitθ​ means a higher effective price, so a subsidised type has sitθ<1s^{\theta}_{it}<1sitθ​<1 and a type that pays more than the market price has sitθ>1s^{\theta}_{it}>1sitθ​>1. For example, with Qit=10Q_{it}=10Qit​=10 and sitθ=0.8s^{\theta}_{it}=0.8sitθ​=0.8 the type pays 888 per unit. The terms are defined up to a normalisation that makes net subsidies sum to zero, so they redistribute between types and do not require outside financing.

Both objects enter the indirect utility (6) and the attractiveness (7). In the calibration the subsidy terms are observed inputs when amenities biθb^{\theta}_ibiθ​ are recovered from residential choices; without them, the sorting of types into subsidised housing would be attributed to amenities.

Two remarks on interpretation. First, the paper treats Uˉtθ\bar{U}^{\theta}_tUˉtθ​ as exogenous in the counterfactuals, which is the assumption that the metropolitan area is too small to move the national sum; strictly, the national sum contains the metropolitan one. In the calibration Uˉtθ\bar{U}^{\theta}_tUˉtθ​ is simply the residual that makes the condition hold at the observed population shares. Second, the right-hand side is the expected utility of a worker restricted to the metropolitan area, taken over all workers of the type. By a standard Frechet property, the average utility of those who actually choose the metropolitan area equals Uˉtθ\bar{U}^{\theta}_tUˉtθ​, the same as for those who stay outside, because selection on the idiosyncratic draw offsets differences in systematic utility. Finally, the condition is not defined at ϵ=1\epsilon=1ϵ=1, where the Gamma term diverges, so the lower end of the robustness range for ϵ\epsilonϵ mentioned in the note has to be read as a value strictly above one.

This is the technology of a firm of type θ\thetaθ located in jjj. Output yjtθy^{\theta}_{jt}yjtθ​ is in units of the single final good, which is costlessly traded and serves as numeraire, so its price is one everywhere. The inputs are the number of workers of the type hCjtθh^{\theta}_{Cjt}hCjtθ​ and commercial floor space lCjtθl^{\theta}_{Cjt}lCjtθ​. TjθT^{\theta}_jTjθ​ is a Hicks-neutral productivity fundamental that is specific to the location and the type and constant over time in the baseline; equation (23) later makes it depend on surrounding employment density. The type index does double duty: a type is a demographic group in a sector, each type has its own firms, and firms of type θ\thetaθ hire only workers of type θ\thetaθ. Types are therefore not substitutes in production, and their only interaction on the production side is the competition for commercial floor space in equation (16).

The function is Cobb-Douglas with constant returns to scale. αθ\alpha_{\theta}αθ​ is the cost share of labour and 1−αθ1-\alpha_{\theta}1−αθ​ the cost share of floor space. The calibration sets αθ=0.75\alpha_{\theta}=0.75αθ​=0.75 for manufacturing types and 0.80.80.8 for service types, so manufacturing uses floor space more intensively, which is the moment the heterogeneity is meant to capture. Constant returns imply zero profits and leave firm size undetermined; only the ratio of inputs and the relation between factor prices are pinned down.

The division of each input by its exponent is a normalisation. It is chosen so that the unit cost function has no constant:

These are the two printed expressions. Because the technology has constant returns, both conditions restrict the same ratio of inputs and say nothing about scale. They are mutually consistent only if the two implied ratios are reciprocals of each other, and this consistency requirement is the zero-profit relation between the floor price and the wage in equation (13).

If the function (11) is differentiated as written, the constants do not disappear. The correct conditions for (11) are derived in the panel for equation (14); they have the factor (1−αθ)/αθ(1-\alpha_{\theta})/\alpha_{\theta}(1−αθ​)/αθ​ outside the bracket and no share parameter inside it. The printed version is therefore an internal inconsistency of the paper between its production function and its first-order conditions. In the calibration the first condition is used with observed employment, the observed floor price and the recovered productivity to obtain commercial floor space by type.

This is the zero-profit floor price as printed in the paper (its equation 7). Like equation (12), it belongs to the technology without normalising constants; the version implied by the production function (11) is the last line of equation (14).

Summing over types and using the fact that the shares ΩRitθ\Omega^{\theta}_{Rit}ΩRitθ​ add up to one gives the condition that determines the housing price of the location: total demand equals the fixed stock lRitl_{Rit}lRit​. With the subsidy terms made explicit, the price is the housing expenditure of all residents, deflated by the subsidy terms, per unit of floor space, which rises one for one with local income and falls one for one with the stock of floor space. This is how a plan that releases land in iii lowers the price there and raises the attractiveness (7).

These are the two no-arbitrage conditions of the floor space markets. Floor space in a location is homogeneous and owned by developers who rent to the highest bidder, so in equilibrium every type that uses floor space in a location must pay the same market price.

On the residential side, QitθQ^{\theta}_{it}Qitθ​ is the price at which the residents of type θ\thetaθ in iii are willing to absorb exactly the share ΩRitθ\Omega^{\theta}_{Rit}ΩRitθ​ of the stock that is allocated to them, obtained by solving equation (15) for the price. Requiring this price to be the same for all types determines the shares: floor space is reallocated towards a type whose implied price is higher until the prices are equal, subject to the shares summing to one. Given the common market price, the shares are simply each type's fraction of total local demand. The subsidy terms of equation (5) still drive a wedge between the common market price QitQ_{it}Qit​ and the effective price each type pays.

Together with commuting market clearing and the open-city condition (10), these conditions close the model whose equilibrium Proposition 1 shows to be unique. In the calibration the second condition is what allows a single observed commercial price per location to identify a productivity for each of the six types.

This is the assumed mapping from travel time to the commuting cost that divides utility in equation (3). τij\tau_{ij}τij​ is the shortest travel time in minutes between residence iii and workplace jjj on the combined road and rail network, and ξθ>0\xi^{\theta}>0ξθ>0 is a type-specific parameter that converts minutes into a utility loss. The cost is an iceberg factor: a commute of τij\tau_{ij}τij​ minutes leaves the worker with the fraction exp⁡(−ξθτij)\exp(-\xi^{\theta}\tau_{ij})exp(−ξθτij​) of the utility of a costless commute.

The exponential form implies a constant semi-elasticity: each additional minute lowers utility by the same proportion, whatever the length of the trip,

∂ln⁡dijθ∂τij=ξθ\frac{\partial\ln d^{\theta}_{ij}}{\partial\tau_{ij}}=\xi^{\theta}∂τij​∂lndijθ​​=ξθ

For illustration, with ξθ=0.01\xi^{\theta}=0.01ξθ=0.01 a 30-minute commute costs 1−e−0.3≈261-e^{-0.3}\approx261−e−0.3≈26 percent of utility. The form is standard in the literature that follows Ahlfeldt, Redding, Sturm and Wolf (2015) for two reasons. Combined with the Frechet shock it gives the log-linear gravity equation (18), in which travel time enters linearly with coefficient −ξθϵ-\xi^{\theta}\epsilon−ξθϵ; and it is defined for short trips, unlike a power function of time. The convention τii=1\tau_{ii}=1τii​=1 gives workers who live and work in the same municipality a small positive cost exp⁡(ξθ)\exp(\xi^{\theta})exp(ξθ) and avoids a zero travel time.

The parameter is not estimated separately. The gravity regression identifies the product ξθϵ\xi^{\theta}\epsilonξθϵ, and ξθ\xi^{\theta}ξθ follows from the value ϵ=6.83\epsilon=6.83ϵ=6.83 taken from the literature. Type heterogeneity in ξθ\xi^{\theta}ξθ is one of the two mechanisms, with type-specific amenities, that limit the gains from co-location. The master plan affects commuting costs only through τij\tau_{ij}τij​: the rapid rail segments chosen in equation (1) lower travel times, and the counterfactual without transport investments recomputes τij\tau_{ij}τij​ on the road network alone.

The gravity equation follows from the commuting probability (8), the attractiveness (7) and the commuting cost (17). Estimation and identification. The equation is estimated for each type in multiplicative form, by Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood and by negative binomial regression, which keeps the pairs with zero flows that the log form would drop. The coefficient is identified from variation in travel time across pairs within a residence and within a workplace. The threat is that fast links were built to connect chosen places, so that travel time is correlated with unobserved bilateral determinants of flows. The paper restricts the sample to pairs of municipalities in the set OOO, which lie on the routes of equation (1) between the centre and a New Town and were connected only incidentally. The semi-elasticities are larger in magnitude in this sample than in the full sample.

This defines the scaled-up plan, the benchmark against which New Towns are evaluated. L~itR,su\tilde{L}^{R,su}_{it}L~itR,su​ is the increment of residential land released in municipality iii in period ttt under this plan; the tilde marks an increment as opposed to the stock. Li,1968RL^R_{i,1968}Li,1968R​ is the stock of residential land in iii in 1968, before the New Towns, so the fraction on the right is the share of municipality iii in the metropolitan land stock of 1968. The last factor is the total amount of new residential land released in the metropolitan area in period ttt.

The rule is proportional allocation: a municipality that held 1 percent of residential land in 1968 receives 1 percent of all new land. If a location held 200 of 10,000 hectares in 1968 and 5,000 hectares are released, it receives 0.02×5,000=1000.02\times5{,}000=1000.02×5,000=100 hectares. Every location grows at the same rate, so the relative land distribution of 1968 is preserved, which is why the plan is read as the status quo strategy.

As written, the total on the right is the sum of the left-hand side over iii, so the equation is formally circular: summing both sides over iii gives an identity. It has to be read with the total as an exogenous number, common to all plans and equal to the total released under the observed New Town plan. Writing this common total as Λt\Lambda_tΛt​ (a symbol not in the note), the rule is

L~itR,su=Li,1968R∑iLi,1968RΛt,Λt=∑iL~itR,su=∑iL~itR,hc=∑iL~itR,us\tilde{L}^{R,su}_{it}=\frac{L^R_{i,1968}}{\sum_iL^R_{i,1968}}\Lambda_t,\qquad\Lambda_t=\sum_i\tilde{L}^{R,su}_{it}=\sum_i\tilde{L}^{R,hc}_{it}=\sum_i\tilde{L}^{R,us}_{it}L~itR,su​=∑i​Li,1968R​Li,1968R​​Λt​,Λt​=i∑​L~itR,su​=i∑​L~itR,hc​=i∑​L~itR,us​

The same rule is applied to commercial land. The increments are added to the 1968 stocks, converted into floor space by equation (2), and the model is solved for the equilibrium of each period. This plan also supplies the part of the hyper-concentration and urban sprawl plans in equations (20) and (21) that is not reallocated. The plans differ only in where land is placed, so differences in outcomes are effects of urban structure together with the induced population response, not of the amount of land.

The hyper-concentration plan reallocates the part of new land that the observed plan puts in New Towns and leaves the rest as in the scaled-up plan. The equation is a definition; what can be derived is that it respects the requirement that all plans release the same total, and that the version printed in the paper does not.

so every location would receive the whole non-reallocated amount and the total would be exceeded. The location-level term used in the note is the reading that adds up. A second point is that the paper introduces sts_tst​ as the land made available in New Towns, a quantity. The formula requires a share between zero and one; if StS_tSt​ denotes the quantity, then st=St/Λts_t=S_t/\Lambda_tst​=St​/Λt​.

Interpretation. The weight ψi\psi_iψi​ is largest for municipalities next to the centre, so the land that went to New Towns 20 to 35 kilometres out is moved towards the historical core. For a municipality 2 kilometres from the centre the weight is ten times that of one 20 kilometres away. The plan represents a monocentric densification strategy and is the polar opposite of the urban sprawl plan in equation (21).

The urban sprawl plan has the same structure as the hyper-concentration plan in equation (20), with the area weight in place of the distance weight. With the common total Λt\Lambda_tΛt​ and sts_tst​ read as a share, as in the panel for equation (20), the plan is

L~itR,us=stai∑iaiΛt+(1−st)L~itR,su\tilde{L}^{R,us}_{it}=s_t\frac{a_i}{\sum_ia_i}\Lambda_t+\left(1-s_t\right)\tilde{L}^{R,su}_{it}L~itR,us​=st​∑i​ai​ai​​Λt​+(1−st​)L~itR,su​

Adding up. The area weights sum to one and the scaled-up increments sum to the common total by equation (19), so

∑iL~itR,us=stΛt∑iai∑iai+(1−st)Λt=Λt\sum_i\tilde{L}^{R,us}_{it}=s_t\Lambda_t\frac{\sum_ia_i}{\sum_ia_i}+\left(1-s_t\right)\Lambda_t=\Lambda_ti∑​L~itR,us​=st​Λt​∑i​ai​∑i​ai​​+(1−st​)Λt​=Λt​

and the total is the same as under the other plans. As for equation (20), the paper (its footnote 35) prints the last term as the metropolitan total (1−st)∑iL~itR,su(1-s_t)\sum_i\tilde{L}^{R,su}_{it}(1−st​)∑i​L~itR,su​, which does not depend on iii and would give a total of stΛt+I(1−st)Λts_t\Lambda_t+I(1-s_t)\Lambda_tst​Λt​+I(1−st​)Λt​; the location-level term is needed.

A numerical illustration with three locations shows the difference. Let the total be Λt=100\Lambda_t=100Λt​=100, the share st=0.4s_t=0.4st​=0.4, the 1968 land shares (0.6,0.3,0.1)(0.6,0.3,0.1)(0.6,0.3,0.1) and the area shares (0.1,0.3,0.6)(0.1,0.3,0.6)(0.1,0.3,0.6). The scaled-up plan gives (60,30,10)(60,30,10)(60,30,10). The sprawl plan gives

0.4×(10,30,60)+0.6×(60,30,10)=(40,30,30)0.4\times\left(10,30,60\right)+0.6\times\left(60,30,10\right)=\left(40,30,30\right)0.4×(10,30,60)+0.6×(60,30,10)=(40,30,30)

which sums to 100100100. With the printed last term every location would receive 0.6×100=600.6\times100=600.6×100=60 in addition to the first part, a total of 220220220.

Interpretation. Area is time-invariant and unrelated to existing density, and the large municipalities are in the periphery, so the reallocated land is spread thinly over the outskirts. Compared with the observed plan, which concentrates this land in five sub-centres connected by rail, the sprawl plan places it where access to jobs is poor. In the results New Towns raise population by 71.81 percent relative to this plan, the largest gap among the three alternatives. The observed plan, hyper-concentration and sprawl thus differ only in the spatial weights applied to the same share sts_tst​ of the same total.

This is the Shannon entropy of the type composition of the residents of location iii, used as a measure of residential mixity (the opposite of segregation). Here πiθ\pi^{\theta}_iπiθ​ is the share of type θ\thetaθ among the residents of iii, so the shares sum to one across the types within a location. This is a different object from the residence probability πitθ\pi^{\theta}_{it}πitθ​ of equation (9), which is the share of all type θ\thetaθ workers who live in iii and sums to one across locations. In terms of resident counts,

πiθ=hiθ∑θ′=1Θhiθ′,∑θ=1Θπiθ=1\pi^{\theta}_i=\frac{h^{\theta}_{i}}{\sum_{\theta'=1}^{\Theta}h^{\theta'}_{i}},\qquad\sum_{\theta=1}^{\Theta}\pi^{\theta}_i=1πiθ​=∑θ′=1Θ​hiθ′​hiθ​​,θ=1∑Θ​πiθ​=1

The upper limit of the sum uses Θ\ThetaΘ for the number of types, six in the application, with the convention that a type with a zero share contributes zero.

The index is zero when all residents of the location are of one type and reaches its maximum when all types are equally represented:

0≤ei≤log⁡Θ,log⁡6≈1.790\leq e_i\leq\log\Theta,\qquad\log6\approx1.790≤ei​≤logΘ,log6≈1.79

For example, with two types the index is log⁡2≈0.69\log2\approx0.69log2≈0.69 for shares (0.5,0.5)(0.5,0.5)(0.5,0.5) and 0.330.330.33 for shares (0.9,0.1)(0.9,0.1)(0.9,0.1). Each term weighs the surprise −log⁡πiθ-\log\pi^{\theta}_i−logπiθ​ of meeting a resident of type θ\thetaθ by the frequency of that type. The index is symmetric in the types and takes no account of which types are similar to each other, so a mix of juniors and seniors in the same sector counts as much as a mix across sectors.

The metropolitan measure is the average of eie_iei​ weighted by residential population. It is an outcome of the counterfactuals, not an input of the model. The New Town plan lowers it by 0.67 percent relative to the scaled-up plan: because amenities biθb^{\theta}_ibiθ​ and commuting costs are type-specific, the new sub-centres attract families and manufacturing workers disproportionately, and neighbourhoods become more homogeneous. Note that the maximum of the index, equal shares of all types, is not the metropolitan composition, so the index measures evenness and not representativeness.

These two equations define the extension with agglomeration economies. The time-invariant fundamentals TjθT^{\theta}_jTjθ​ and biθb^{\theta}_ibiθ​ of the baseline are multiplied by spillover terms, so that productivity TjtθT^{\theta}_{jt}Tjtθ​ and amenity bitθb^{\theta}_{it}bitθ​ become endogenous and time-varying.

The production spillover at workplace jjj is a travel-time weighted sum, over all locations kkk, of the density of type θ\thetaθ employment per unit of commercial floor space used by the type. The weight e−δτjke^{-\delta\tau_{jk}}e−δτjk​ falls with the travel time between jjj and kkk at rate δ\deltaδ, and λ\lambdaλ is the elasticity of productivity with respect to the weighted density. The residential spillover at residence iii has the same form with the density of type θ\thetaθ residents per unit of residential floor space, decay ρ\rhoρ and elasticity η\etaη. With λ=η=0\lambda=\eta=0λ=η=0 the baseline is recovered. Spillovers operate within a type only: the density of other types does not enter.

What the paper prints (its equation 9) uses the location's own index as the index of summation: the sum for productivity runs over jjj with weight e−δτjie^{-\delta\tau_{ji}}e−δτji​ and density indexed by jjj, and the sum for amenities runs over iii with weight e−ρτije^{-\rho\tau_{ij}}e−ρτij​ and density indexed by iii. Read literally, the left-hand side index would be bound by the sum and the result would not depend on the location, apart from a free index in the travel time. The intended expression, as in Ahlfeldt, Redding, Sturm and Wolf (2015), is the one in the note with a separate summation index kkk.

The decay parameters are δ=0.98\delta=0.98δ=0.98 and ρ=0.55\rho=0.55ρ=0.55 per minute, so the weights fall quickly:

e−0.98×5≈0.007,e−0.55×5≈0.064e^{-0.98\times5}\approx0.007,\qquad e^{-0.55\times5}\approx0.064e−0.98×5≈0.007,e−0.55×5≈0.064

A location five minutes away receives a weight below 1 percent in production and about 6 percent in amenities; spillovers are very local, and the own-location term has weight e−δe^{-\delta}e−δ or e−ρe^{-\rho}e−ρ because τii=1\tau_{ii}=1τii​=1. This locality is why New Towns can build up their own density without depending on the centre.

Substituting these terms into equations (7) and (13) creates a feedback: more workers raise productivity and wages, which attract more workers. The dispersion forces that guarantee uniqueness in Proposition 1 may then be dominated, which is why spillovers are left out of the baseline. In the exercise the model is recalibrated for each pair of elasticities, including the fundamentals and the reservation utilities of equation (10), so that every version matches the observed data and only the counterfactual responses differ. The gains from New Towns increase with λ\lambdaλ and η\etaη.

This is the event-study difference-in-differences specification for the Paris municipalities. yity_{it}yit​ is an outcome of municipality iii in census year ttt, such as population or the share of a demographic group or sector. μi\mu_iμi​ is a municipality fixed effect that absorbs permanent differences in levels, ηt\eta_tηt​ is a census-year effect common to all municipalities, and uitu_{it}uit​ is the error. The treated units are the municipalities of the five New Towns, and the controls are the municipalities of New Towns that were planned and then discarded, which were judged suitable by the same planners.

The notation is compressed, since the index of summation has the same name as the time index of the observation. Written out with a separate index rrr for the years of the sum and a time-invariant treatment indicator NiN_iNi​ (neither is in the note), the regressors are

Dir,t=Ni×1{t=r},yit=∑r≠1962βrDir,t+μi+ηt+uitD_{ir,t}=N_i\times\mathbf{1}\{t=r\},\qquad y_{it}=\sum_{r\neq1962}\beta_rD_{ir,t}+\mu_i+\eta_t+u_{it}Dir,t​=Ni​×1{t=r},yit​=r=1962∑​βr​Dir,t​+μi​+ηt​+uit​

so for an observation in year ttt only the term with r=tr=tr=t is switched on. The reference year 1962, the last census before the plan, is omitted, because the full set of interactions would be collinear with the municipality fixed effects.

Each coefficient is a difference in differences:

βt=(E[yit∣Ni=1]−E[yi,1962∣Ni=1])−(E[yit∣Ni=0]−E[yi,1962∣Ni=0])\beta_t=\left(\mathbb{E}\left[y_{it}|N_i=1\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[y_{i,1962}|N_i=1\right]\right)-\left(\mathbb{E}\left[y_{it}|N_i=0\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[y_{i,1962}|N_i=0\right]\right)βt​=(E[yit​∣Ni​=1]−E[yi,1962​∣Ni​=1])−(E[yit​∣Ni​=0]−E[yi,1962​∣Ni​=0])

It is identified from within-municipality changes relative to 1962, compared between treated and control municipalities. The identifying assumption is parallel trends: without the plan, the built and the discarded New Towns would have evolved alike. Coefficients for years before 1962, where available, serve as a check. Because all five New Towns start at the same time, there is no staggered adoption problem.

The estimates are descriptive facts that motivate the model: strong population growth in New Towns and rising shares of families and manufacturing workers. They compare locations within the metropolitan area and so cannot tell whether New Towns added population to the area or relocated it, nor can they separate the effect of land from that of transport. That is the role of the structural counterfactuals built on equations (19) to (21).

This is the event-study specification for the worldwide sample, used to assess external validity. The unit iii is a night-light cell of about one square kilometre inside an urban area, ttt is a calendar year between 1992 and 2012, and ppp is event time, the number of years relative to the opening of the New Town in the cell's urban area (pooled into bins). yitpy_{itp}yitp​ is the luminosity of the cell, μi\mu_iμi​ a cell fixed effect, ηt\eta_tηt​ a year fixed effect and uitpu_{itp}uitp​ the error. DipD_{ip}Dip​ interacts the treatment status of the urban area with an indicator for event-time bin ppp. As in equation (24), the index of summation shares its name with the event time of the observation, and one bin is omitted as the reference.

The coefficients βp\beta_pβp​ trace the path of log luminosity in treated urban areas relative to urban areas that never receive a New Town, before and after the opening. Unlike equation (24), treatment is staggered, since the 314 New Towns open in different years, so calendar-year effects and event-time effects are separately identified, with the never-treated areas pinning down the year effects. Identification rests on parallel trends in log luminosity. The pre-opening coefficients are flat until about four years before the opening, which is consistent with construction starting before the administrative opening date.

Because the outcome is in logs, a coefficient is a log difference. Ten years after the opening the coefficient is about 0.30.30.3, and the conversion to GDP uses the elasticity of GDP with respect to night lights of 0.30.30.3 from Henderson, Storeygard and Weil (2012):

e0.3−1≈0.35,0.35×0.3≈0.105e^{0.3}-1\approx0.35,\qquad0.35\times0.3\approx0.105e0.3−1≈0.35,0.35×0.3≈0.105

that is, luminosity about 35 percent higher and GDP about 10.5 percent higher, close to the 11.4 percent of the structural model for Paris. The comparison is between a reduced-form effect for whole urban areas and the model's metropolitan effect, so it speaks to the aggregate effect and not to relocation within an area.

The specification is called the initial model because luminosity is recorded on a scale with a floor and a ceiling. Estimating it by least squares ignores the censoring described in equation (26) and biases the effects towards zero; the paper's preferred estimates use the Tobit version.

This is the observation rule of a two-limit Tobit model. The satellite data record night-time luminosity as an integer between 0 and 63. A cell that is darker than the sensor's detection threshold is recorded as 0, and a cell brighter than the saturation level is recorded as 63, which is common in the centres of large cities. lit∗l^*_{it}lit∗​ is the latent, uncensored luminosity, assumed to be normally distributed around a linear index, and litl_{it}lit​ is what is observed. The observation equals the latent variable inside the interval and is stacked at the limits outside it.

Let the latent variable have conditional mean mitm_{it}mit​, given by the right-hand side of equation (25), and standard deviation σ\sigmaσ (symbols not in the note), and let φ\varphiφ and Φ\PhiΦ be the standard normal density and distribution function. The likelihood contribution of an observation has three parts:

Pr⁡(lit=0)=Φ(0−mitσ),f(lit)=1σφ(lit−mitσ) for 0<lit<63,Pr⁡(lit=63)=1−Φ(63−mitσ)\Pr\left(l_{it}=0\right)=\Phi\left(\frac{0-m_{it}}{\sigma}\right),\qquad f\left(l_{it}\right)=\frac{1}{\sigma}\varphi\left(\frac{l_{it}-m_{it}}{\sigma}\right)\ \text{for }0<l_{it}<63,\qquad\Pr\left(l_{it}=63\right)=1-\Phi\left(\frac{63-m_{it}}{\sigma}\right)Pr(lit​=0)=Φ(σ0−mit​​),f(lit​)=σ1​φ(σlit​−mit​​) for 0<lit​<63,Pr(lit​=63)=1−Φ(σ63−mit​​)

Maximum likelihood uses the density for interior observations and the two probabilities for observations at the limits, and so recovers the parameters of the latent mean.

Why this matters: at a limit the observed variable cannot move. A cell that is already saturated shows no increase when a New Town raises activity, and a dark cell that brightens but stays below the detection threshold shows none either. Least squares on the observed variable averages these zero responses with the true ones and understates the effect, which is what the paper finds: estimators that ignore the censoring give smaller coefficients. The effect on the observed mean is the latent effect scaled by the probability of being uncensored,

∂E[lit]∂mit=Φ(63−mitσ)−Φ(0−mitσ)<1\frac{\partial\mathbb{E}\left[l_{it}\right]}{\partial m_{it}}=\Phi\left(\frac{63-m_{it}}{\sigma}\right)-\Phi\left(\frac{0-m_{it}}{\sigma}\right)<1∂mit​∂E[lit​]​=Φ(σ63−mit​​)−Φ(σ0−mit​​)<1

The cost of the Tobit is its reliance on normality and homoskedasticity of the latent error, and the many cell fixed effects of equation (25) raise an incidental parameters concern in a nonlinear model. One detail is left open by the paper: the regression (25) is written for the logarithm of luminosity, while the censoring points are stated for the level, and the logarithm of a zero reading is not defined; the paper does not say how the two are reconciled.
